Is he not her own descendant?
Let her take comfort in the child
Who remains after me!”
He murmured and rumbled,
And before the noble hero finished his last wishes,
Kanchoro, son of Chubak—
Alas, that troublemaking Choro—
Appeared ahead with a multitude.
Damn you, Kanchoro—
God surely exists, you traitor to your salt!
The earth churned beneath the teeming host;
He drove an army too vast for the land,
Driving all the troops together.
On the crest of a forked ridge,
Toward your prince standing gaunt,
Stripped of his steed,
Toward your prince standing there exposed,
They loosed their bows like pouring rain
And shot their arrows like hail.
With vigilant Kanchoro at their head,
They had chosen the path of treachery
And wrought a strange spectacle.
The great host of the Black Jediger,
Led by Kyyaz and Kanchoro,
Crossed the low, tawny foothill plain,
Advancing until they arrived.
When the vast army in its tens of thousands
Surged over the land and arrived,
The lone hero paced slowly, conserving his strength,
And reverence came over him;
The solitary gray-maned lion,
Leaning upon Akkelte,
Showed the mettle of a wolf
As he climbed untroubled
Onto a saddle-backed ridge.
He cared no more that the Jediger might engulf him
Than if they touched the hem of his robe.
Courage and defiant pride
Had been fashioned by my Lord,
Who had granted them without measure.
At the sight of the khan, the Jediger host
Burned inwardly with raging flame.
Deeply distressed, they raised an uproar,
Unable either to advance across the ridge
Toward Kyyaz and Kanchoro,
For fear had seized the multitude,
Or to turn back and flee;
Nor could they lower their spears with a battle cry
And overwhelm the lionhearted hero.
Confounded and anguished,
The multitude stood in an uproar.
Despairing of their borrowed lives, they said,
“He was our father—how could we
Have begun a battle against the bloody-handed hero?
When there are no black Manchus or Chinese here,
How could we take the head
Of the hero who was our protector?”
The people stirred and clamored,
And the ignorant repeated what the knowing said,
Whispering softly among themselves:
“His father was Manas, the gray-maned hero,
Born in Altai
When the Kyrgyz had been taken captive.
At twelve years of age,
He toppled kingdoms and took spoils,
And set the whole world in turmoil.
He was the hero who brought back
The Kyrgyz taken away to China.
To this scattered, dwindling people
He was like a father.
Oh, what can we do against this gray-maned lion?
He is the offspring of a lion,
A forested cape that scatters
The wind when storms descend.
He was a shield for multitudes;
Your blue-maned lion of a hero was a fortress.
People, let us scatter grain as an offering
And not assail that noble hero;
Let all the Jediger standing here
Rise as one and flee!
Their first forefather was Karagan;
When mighty Karagan died,
Many Kyrgyz were taken captive
And scattered to various lands.
When that Karagan died
And the enemy pressed in,
They slaughtered many of your elders,
Leaving all your yurt poles red with blood.
They carried your daughters off as spoil
After eating your salt countless times;
They destroyed your villages
And brutally cut open
Your pregnant wives.
Think, all you people—
Do you still remember
How they destroyed so many of your young,
And carried your leaders off as captives?
They shattered your nation
And seized your land,
Dear to you as the ancestral mountains.
They demanded the lives of your young,
And divided your leaders among distant lands:
Some they drove to Altai,
Some they drove to Kanghai;
Half of us went to Eyren,
And most of us fell into an abyss.
Many of us went among the Kazakhs,
And most of us fell into misery.
Then his father, the hero Manas, arose
And came yesterday to settle in Talas.
When your Manas became the great Manas,
When he donned his invulnerable coat,
Mounted his horse with legs spread wide,
And rode his steed Akkula,
No land remained where Akkula had not trod.
No nation remained whole
That Khan Manas had not conquered.
That cherished land of Jetisuu
Manas gave you and made your homeland.
Delivering you from the infidel,
Greathearted Manas made you a nation.
How can we, his people, march against
The gray-maned son of Manas?
How can we betray the salt
Of the gray-maned hero now gone?
Have you no shame, Kyrgyz people?
How can we attack his son?
With what face can we now strike
The bloody-handed hero who shielded so many?
Let us cross the foothill ridge;
Come, people, let us divide and flee
Without attacking or assailing the hero!
Here, let us cross the Jorgo Pass;
Come, people, let us flee without approaching him!
Let us cross the Beshtash Pass;
Come, people, let us flee without confronting him.
How can we heed a slave false to his salt
And attack the hero from the side?
How can we heed that arrogant dog
And strike the gray-maned lion?”
The Jediger halted without crossing
The saddle-backed ridge;
The Jediger dared not advance
Against the gray-maned son of Manas.
Though Kanchoro and Kyyaz shouted,
Calling on them to surge forward,
They wondered how they could dishonor
Manas, who had gone to the other world,
And the Jediger would not attack.
While the Jediger still held back,
Before another word could be said,
In the time it takes to blink,
From the meadows of Jylgynduu and Keng-Kol,
From the lower reaches of Talas,
An astonishing cloud of dust billowed up,
With shouting mingled in the dust.
When they listened to the shouting,
The war cry “Manas!” rang out.
The sight stirred every heart:
A figure loomed like a mountain.
Like the depths of a narrow river,
His valor was beyond compare;
He resembled an angel of death.
His brows were like a crouching hound,
His head was as great as a cauldron,
And upon each of his two shoulders
Two giants might have perched.
He looked able to slaughter all he met;
“Manas!” was his battle cry,
And his full eyes were broad as bowls.
His manly strength was immense;
Once he seized a foe, he never let him go,
And seemed able to swallow both slaves whole.
His mottled eyes bulged fiercely;
The jutting boss of his shield
Made the heart quail.
He was himself a warrior against warring foes;
If you have not heard of him,
He was Sary Khan’s own beloved son.
“If fate decrees it, I shall die;
I shall go as a supporting force
For the hero Semetey.”
Blood veiled his dark eyes,
And radiance lit his blood-red face.
Like a cloud breaking over a ridge,
With piercing cries and hoarse shouts,
Sary Khan came into sight.
His little banner streamed,
And he crushed all he encountered.
The club-like flesh of either cheek
Could have fed two lions;
If he passed through ten thousand troops on either side,
He looked able to slaughter them all.
He loomed like a high riverbank,
His figure towering like a mountain.
When you looked at his nose,
It was like the sheath of a saber;
His bristling mustache
Was like a Bukhara sword.
His temples were like rounded boulders,
And the hollows of his two eyes
Like pits dug by laborers.
Then Sary Khan arrived,
His little banner streaming,
Crushing all he met.
Sary Khan was a master spearman,
Truly skilled at finding advantage,
Most accomplished in stratagem,
And mighty as well.
Broad-jawed and free of tongue,
He was eloquent as well;
Sary Khan, wolf of war,
Was farsighted too.
Sary Khan charged in with a roar,
Calling, “Slaughter those who oppose you!
Drive your spears into the enemy!”
The great host of the Black Jediger
Split cleanly apart and scattered.
“Kanchoro and Kyyaz, those two traitors,
Are driving us here by force,” they said,
And clamored as they told
Their sorrows to mighty Sary Khan:
“We dwelt at ease in Jetisuu,
Calling him the son of the peerless hero,
But those two traitors drove us here under duress.
The Jediger in Jetisuu,
While the bloody-handed hero Manas lived,
Were a free people in a peaceful land.
We Jediger in Jetisuu
Were a free people whom not even
The slightest breeze dared touch.
We drank kumiss and courted girls,
Played knucklebones and the game of ordo,
Played chess and reveled noisily,
Rode young horses and hunted with birds;
We too were a people living in carefree splendor.
Then dust rose from Jeti-Özön—
Kanchoro and Kyyaz emerged as khans,
And the cries of those two accursed dogs
Nearly frightened the life from us.
We have no sword belts buckled for battle,
And no enemy among the red-tasseled Chinese
With whom we must fight to the death.
We have not even the smallest claim for money
Against the hero, Manas’s son.
We, the great host of the Black Jediger,
Were forced into this invasion
And now stand here suffering;
Our khan has proved a fool.
We, the great host of the Black Jediger—
What can we possibly do?
Can anyone prosper who shoots at
The hero who has gone to the other world?
Can any two men prevail in combat
Against the bloody-handed hero who protected us?
